<!-- The record test of 2026-10-13 kept as a kit to run again: ten scenarios over the entries of the record rule's trial, their key and rubric, the script that fills them from a copy of the repository, the reader's and the grader's briefs, and the blind grading of the first run. -->

# The record test, a kit

The test asks whether a worker or the coordinator decides as well from entries written to the record rule as from the old ones. The new texts are Parts 3 and 3b of `../record-rule-draft.md`, and the first run's result is its Part 4. Scenarios 9 and 10 test the pairs of Part 3b, an entry of POSITIONS with the FACTS entries that build it.

## The files

- `questions.md`: the ten scenarios. A `{FACTS n}` or `{POSITIONS n}` line stands for the entry numbered `F-n` or `P-n`, which was the entry on line n when the record was numbered.
- `key.md`: for each scenario, the right answer, the facts it rests on and where they live, the wrong answers, and the rubric (decision 0 to 2, sources 0 to 1). Its notes on scenarios 9 and 10 say what the duplication between FACTS and POSITIONS did. It is kept as the first run used it. `grades.md` § 5 lists seven slips that the grader found in it.
- `fill.py`: fills the questions from one copy.
- `brief-reader.md`: the reader's brief, with `@DIR@`, `@QUESTIONS@` and `@OUT@` to fill in.
- `brief-grader.md`: the grader's brief. It names the first run's scratch folder; put yours in its place.
- `grades.md`: the first run's blind grading. X is the new entries and Y the old.
- `grades-pilot.md`: the second run's grading, on the consolidation's pilot: one reader in the pilot's copy, graded against the first run's old-entries answers. X is the old entries and Y the pilot's; 28 and 29 of 30.
- `grades-final.md`: the third run's grading, on the finished consolidation: one reader in its copy, graded against the first run's old-entries answers. X is the finished record and Y the old entries; 30 and 28 of 30.
- `grades-scenario6.md`: scenario 6 run again on the final record (124.1K), its entry F-201 replaced by the `coordinator` skill's section that now holds it; graded by the coordinator, not blind: 3 of 3, as before.

## How to run it

1. Make two worktrees of `main` at one base, detached: `git worktree add --detach /home/user/record-test-p BASE`, and the same for `/home/user/record-test-q`. Copy p keeps the old entries; copy q gets the new ones.
2. In both copies, delete what would tell a reader about the test or show it the other copy's texts, and commit nothing: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, `HELD.md`, `process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md`, this folder, and their lines in `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`.
3. In copy q, put in the new texts. Replace each entry's line with its new text from Part 3, or from Part 3b where the entry is there too, as POSITIONS 48 and 60 are. Write each one with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py set` in the copy, which keeps the old line in the history file. Then run `record.py check --base HEAD` in the copy.
4. Check the placeholders. `questions.md` names each entry by its line number at `0f54a698b`, which is its number since the record was numbered. On another base, check that each number still names the entry that the scenario means (the titles in Parts 3 and 3b; a merged entry's number is gone), and change the number where it does not. `fill.py` checks only that the number names one entry.
5. Fill the questions, once for each copy, into a file outside both copies: `python3 fill.py /home/user/record-test-p questions.md OUT`.
6. Launch one fresh Opus reader in each copy, with `brief-reader.md`: `@DIR@` is the copy, `@QUESTIONS@` its filled questions, `@OUT@` its answers. The two briefs differ in nothing else. Each reader wrote about 0.4M tokens in the first run.
7. Blind the answers. Copy them to `grade/answers-X.md` and `grade/answers-Y.md` by a choice the grader does not see, and write which is which in a file that the grader is not given (`arms.txt` in the first run).
8. Launch one Fable grader with `brief-grader.md`. It reads `questions.md` unfilled, `key.md` and the two answer files, and checks against `main` any claim beyond the key. It wrote 0.75M tokens in the first run.
9. Unblind with the arms file, and report by "the new entries" and "the old entries", not X and Y.

To re-run one scenario after an entry is repaired, cut `questions.md` to that scenario, fill it from the copy, and give a fresh reader the same brief. Grade it against the same key. In the first run, the coordinator graded the re-run of scenario 7 itself, knowing its copy, so that grade was not blind.

# F-63 traced: where it came from, what it is, how common it is

## In short

1. F-63 was written on 2026-09-22 by the gather agent of climb batch 3, for rung L, a rung that repaired five defects that the compiled checker found in the one library's api files; the rung's brief asked for "the FACTS.md line or lines this rung earns", and the gather put each line in as "one bullet".
2. Its first title was "Rung L of climb batch 3 repaired the interpreter library's five plain api defects ...": it reported one rung's work, not one property of the tree.
3. Eleven rewrites from 2026-09-24 to 10-13 removed the repairs that later work replaced and gave the bullet a title that lists what still stands, but none of them split it.
4. Of its eleven history blocks, one is the numbering, one cuts it to the form, one corrects its evidence, and eight only move two line numbers.
5. The numbering block names none of its nine earlier texts: the numbering script linked old texts by title, and the title had changed that morning, so only git links F-63 to rung L's first text.
6. Its four statements (`String`'s `split` pair, `List`'s missing `zip`, `Condition.map`'s return type, `QQ`'s `comprises { ... }`) share only that each is an api line that rung L changed; each answers its own question, and they changed apart.
7. By the record's six checks it fails ownership, present meaning and comprehension, and its evidence is in part unresolved.
8. Three of its statements are notes on a past repair or on a worker's choice; only the `QQ` sentence bears on an open defect, row 354, through F-64.
9. No FACTS or POSITIONS entry, PLAN item, review-queue item, skill or batch brief cites it; one later probe used its `Condition.map` sentence as a precedent, one audit used its `zip` sentence, and the batches since have only moved its line numbers.
10. In a sample of 40 entries, 2 are of F-63's kind (F-83, F-374), and a third (F-281) adds claims on other subjects from its rung; but 38 of the 40 hold two or more claims that answer different questions, and 24 carry a defect beside the property that their title states.
11. Today the batch brief asks each rung for "The FACTS.md entry the rung earns", the gather adds it "after the section's last entry", and the record-landing workflow rewrites each entry that it is given as one new line.
12. Only the coordinator skill's `record.md` asks the writer to split an entry by question and to look first for the entry that owns the claim; no brief of a rung, of the gather, of the commit stage or of the record-landing sorter or checker asks for either, and the landing's entries writer meets that rule only by a reference, with one new line per entry as its output.

## 2. F-63 by the record's own definitions

### 2.1 A finding and a fact

`fortress-repo`'s `records.md:7`: "A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification ..., a measurement." `:9`: "A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row."

- On 2026-09-22 each of the four statements was a finding of rung L: a defect of the api, measured (`split`, `zip`; `REPORT.md:32`) or read (`Condition.map`), with the rung's choice of repair.
- Each was repaired in the rung, "home 1, repaired" (`REPORT.md:62-66`), so none has a ledger row and none is open. What F-63 holds today is the state of four api lines after their repair.
- To the curator's question, "a defect about interpreters or one library's API?": neither an open defect nor walk's. They are four lines of the one library's api, which only the compiled checker reads (`REPORT.md:74`).

### 2.2 What an entry holds

`coordinator`'s `record.md:18`: "A FACTS entry holds ...: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence ...; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail."

F-63 has what is established now, its evidence and its report sections. What it means for the work is stated only for `QQ` ("No api-declared type extends `QQ`, so F-64's refusal ... does not arise"). It builds no decision. `record.md:29`: "An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own ... Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there." F-63's claims answer four questions and changed apart (1.6).

content.content:
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.

- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).

- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, save two generic ones one inside the other, which stop with an error when an extending object's first instance is made (F-405), and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains), except two whose bounds differ only in the api of a type of one simple name, of which the object's is kept (row 1134). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 and 5.5.

- F-43 **The overloading checker's memo hides some errors, and which ones changes from one build of the checker to another, so the gate's checker count and distance run with the memo off.** The memo keeps a "valid" verdict per pair of declarations. A pair that several traits inherit is checked once per trait, at that trait's instantiation, in hash-set order, so a pair valid for one trait is taken as valid for the next (`perf-probes/nat/triage.md` section 1). The memo is on by default (`OverloadingChecker.scala:79`), so an ordinary `fortress compile` can miss these errors. The JVM property `-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false` turns it off; the gate's checker count and distance stages set it.

- F-47 **The exclusion rule refuses some of the specification's own examples; in their place, a parametric object with a factory, or a widening function, runs on both paths as a user program.** The refused examples are E1 to E10 of `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, "What was found": among them three `where`-clause examples, the Working Draft's `Nothing`, the nested number tower and `RationalQuantity`. The `where`-clause examples stop on both paths before the rule, in name resolution, at `T is undefined`. The alternatives were measured as user programs that declare their own types: a parametric object with a factory, such as `object Empty[\T\]` with `emptyList[\E\]()`, and a widening function, such as `widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\]`. The library's `Nothing[\String\]` does not yet run on the compiled path's prelude (row 331, F-167). A marker object with a `coerce` in the generic trait, as `AltEmptyCoerce` has in `SList[\T\]`, also runs compiled, and walk applies such a coercion (row 389). The 2012 `covariant` keyword passes the compiled checker and dies at run time (row 404). The compiled checker refuses a coercion with its own static parameter between two instantiations, `coerce[\S extends T\](c: C[\S\])`, as a cyclic hierarchy. Inferred from the forest rule: route C (F-46) would rescue neither the `where`-clause examples, `Nothing` nor E8, the internal appendix's "Disjunctive Constraints"; only the tower (E5) and the root `Object`'s algebra (E7) would keep their original text under it. Detail: the same note.

- F-101 **`harness-one.sh` keeps its Fortress cache between calls.** The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh`, and its cache is the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It reuses the cache while the built implementation and the Fortress sources on the source path are those that filled it. `COLD_CACHE=1` empties it first. Detail: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` sections 1 and 4.

- F-103 **The `XXX` expected-failure mechanism in `compiler_tests/` and `library_tests/` cannot express, in one `.test` file, a program that compiles and then fails at run time.** The `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name makes every command that the file drives a must-fail. So such a defect needs two `.test` files over one component: a plain-named file that drives `link`, and an `XXX` file that drives `run` (the `fortress-repo` skill's `tests-writing.md`, "Writing an `XXX` test"). A compile-stage failure needs one `XXX` compile test. An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key whose program compiles is red: "Saw wrong failure". Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-tryatomic/REPORT.md`, "The measured defect, and its home".

- F-107 **Three heaps run the interpreter, and a gated test can pass at two of them and die at the third.** `bin/fortress` gives walk's JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set (row 67: a 2M-element array exhausts it). The harness runs each walk test inside its JUnit JVM, at 768 MB (`junitMem` in `build.xml`). `env.sh` and the `fortress-repo` skill's setup lines set `JAVA_FLAGS` to 4 GB with 64 MB stacks. Measure a claim about a walk failure near a memory limit at 256 MB. A compiled run is not one of the three: `bin/fortress run` goes through `bin/run`, which gives 1536 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set, and `testFast` gives a compiled test's run step 4 GB with 64 MB stacks (F-99). Evidence: observed: before its repair, `IntSemanticsRungI.fss` passed at 4 GB and at 768 MB and died with `OutOfMemoryError` at 256 MB (`compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` sections 3 and 4.4).

- F-145 **Walk refuses at load an object that leaves an inherited abstract method uncovered.** Bodies at narrower parameter types define an abstract method only where together they cover its parameter types, with `comprises` clauses read, as P-147 decides: each position is split through the clauses, and every combination of parts must lie inside one body. A search that does not settle refuses the object: a cycle, a symbolic type or a type that the search cannot read, 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations. A generic object is not checked (row 665). An object whose one covering definition has a static parameter of its own is refused, though it is valid (row 728, a defect of walk; the compiled path runs it). The compiled checker covers the same way, within the same bounds, except that where the abstract method or a body below it has static parameters of its own, it does not split the parameter types, so it refuses an object whose cover needs a split (row 725). Walk's `override` check at load is F-147's, and its check of the Meet Rule for Functional Methods is F-142's. Gated by `tests/AbstractMethod*Walk` (`AbstractMethodCoverUnsettledWalk` among them) and `compiler_tests/AbstractMethodCoveredPairs`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6 (the cover); `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8 (the refusal of a search that does not settle).

- F-147 **Walk refuses an `override` that overrides nothing; an inherited declaration is overridden where each of its parameter types, not counting the self parameter, is a subtype of the `override`'s and not all are equal.** This is the traits chapter's "strict subtype" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:585-589`). At an instance of a generic trait that an object without static parameters extends, equal parameter types still count as overridden (`OverrideGenericInstanceEqualTypesWalk`). Walk checks the `override` of a generic trait, object or object expression once, at its declaration. An object inherits nothing that a trait's `override` overrides, so an object below an abstract `override` that declares no body is refused at load (rows 614, 649; `AbstractOverrideUndefinedWalk`, "does not define an abstract method declared in type W"). Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in an object expression, which takes them from the function around it, or in a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause. There it accepts an `override` over an inherited declaration whose parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s (row 693). The `fortress-repo` skill gives the rule's cases (`references/interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"). Gated by `tests/Override*Walk.fss` and `AbstractOverrideUndefinedWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-override/REPORT.md` section 1.

content.content:
- F-141 **Under `walk`, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes takes its declared bound, and a lone one with no narrowest candidate takes its bound where every argument is below it.** It builds P-48. A lone type parameter is one that is the whole declared type of some argument and that no other argument fixes (F-137); where some argument is not below its bound, it takes the arguments' join. A type parameter that the declared parameter types mention only in function domains, an odd number of arrows deep and never inside a static argument, as `T` in `g: T -> ZZ32`, is bounded by the arguments only from above. Where nothing bounds it from below, it takes the meet of its declared bound and the bounds that the arguments place on it. An F-bounded parameter stays open (F-143). A reduction or comprehension that writes no static argument fixes its big operator's parameter by the declared type of its value, else by its elements' join (F-228). That rule is the coordinator's call. Two more rules are defaults of the walk-instance rung's decision record. First, a parameter that only another fixed parameter's bound mentions takes that parameter's instance, not its own bound: `ap[\T, A extends T\](a: A)` gives `T` the type of `a` (D3, row 592). Second, a lone one whose bound mentions a static parameter has the arguments' supertypes among its candidates, and so takes their narrowest common supertype, never its bound (D5). Defects, each with an expected failure: two bounds that walk cannot meet (row 591); a bound only from above that mentions another static parameter, which keeps `Bottom` (walk's `BottomType`) (row 612); two upper bounds from two function arguments that walk cannot meet, which fail the call (row 616); a parameter that only the result of a function expression with no declared return type fixes, which takes `Bottom` (row 587); a generic passed over at dispatch when its arguments have several minimal common supertypes (row 589), whose repair changes which declaration runs, the curator's to decide. Gated by `tests/Infer*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-instance/REPORT.md` section 2 and its `decision-record.md` section 2; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` section 1; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-meet/REPORT.md` section 1.

- F-143 **Under walk, a type parameter whose bound mentions itself and that nothing at a call fixes is left open.** Such a bound is an F-bound, as in `mk[\T extends Cmp[\T\]\]()`. The open type, printed `OPEN`, is below every type, and every value matches it. A reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument is first instantiated by its declared type or by its elements' join (F-228). So the open parameter reaches one only where neither fixes it: an empty `SUM` or `PROD` that no declared type directs, which takes `ZZ32`'s identity whatever its body's type (row 716), or a clause form whose declared type or join does not fit the bound (F-228). A call such as `mk()` also leaves it open. Where overloads are compared, a tuple, arrow or generic type that holds the open type admits no more than it would at `BottomType`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` does not take `(1, 2)`, though a lone `one(x: (T,T))` does (row 663, contested). In a probe by the rung's skeptic, the agent that checks a rung's work after its worker, a method declared over `T` in an object whose `T` stayed open was the most specific one, and so was chosen for every argument; no gated test holds this. A list comprehension written at such an open parameter, as `<|[\T\] x | x <- xs |>`, ends in `CastError` at its unwrap's cast, `cast[\CovariantCollection[\T\]\](cc)` (`Library/List.fss:179`), and so does `List`'s range subscript at a stride other than 1 on a list of that open element type, since the subscript writes `[\E\]` (row 825, contested). Gated by `tests/InferUnfixedFBoundedWalk.fss`, `OpenTupleDispatchWalk.fss` and `OpenParameterListComprehensionWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-open-param/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 11; its `SKEPTIC.md` section 3, finding 3 (the probe); `compile-ladder/rung-body-arguments/SKEPTIC.md` section 3.

- F-228 **Under walk, a reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument instantiates its big operator by a declared type, else by the join of its elements' run-time types, else at its bound, where an F-bounded parameter stays open.** It builds P-48. The declared type is a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's declared return type, for either also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a top-level variable, a field, an assignment, a function expression, a branch, a call's argument and another clause form's body do not direct it. Otherwise the clauses run once into the library's collector, `__elemsOf`, which keeps the elements in order, typed at the join of their run-time types, and the operator is instantiated at that join; the reduction then runs over the collected elements, so each body runs once. A declared type or a join that does not fit falls back to the instance that no hint gives: a plain-bounded parameter takes its bound, and an F-bounded one stays open (F-143). So a `SUM` of `ZZ32` and `RR64` values, whose join `Number` is outside the bound, runs with each `+` at its operands' types. The same holds with no element and no declared type. With the big operator so instantiated, the library types `__bigOperator`'s local function `body(i: I)` at the element type `I`. A big operator whose declared result is a trait of its own is read through the `BigReduction`, `Comprehension` or `BigOperator` that the trait extends (row 718, fixed). Still wrong, each a ledger row: an empty clause form that no declared type directs takes its bound or stays open (row 716); a comprehension that no declared type reaches is built at the join of its elements' run-time types, which a declared `List[\Shape\]` refuses where its elements are all `Circle`s (row 717); a clause form that is a call's argument gets no declared type (rows 510, 705). Gated by `tests/UnwrittenListMapComprehensionWalk`, `UnwrittenComprehension*Walk`, `ComprehensionTypedBindingWalk`, `UnwrittenSetBigOperatorsWalk`, `UnwrittenEmptyFloatSumWalk`, `IntMapComprehensionTypedWalk` and `UserBigOperatorResultTraitWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` sections 1, 5 (5.3 lists the contexts) and 10, decision 6; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-overload-if/REPORT.md` section 1, "Row 718".

- F-258 **Walk and the compiled checker read exclusion between two declarations, one or both with static parameters, over the whole parameter type, by existential reduction.** A value of both declared domains has, at each position, one instance of each generic type that the two parameter types there are or extend, so those instances' static arguments are equal; the two domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where, at the instance they force, the parameter types at some position exclude. Walk: the Meet branches of `genericPairValid` and of `validOnDeclaredDomains`'s generic-beside-plain reading also ask `domainsExcludeTogether` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:935` at `a93fb3bfd`), which reads bounds where `mayBeEqual` and `meetParams` read them and reads no `where` clause, varargs or lists of different lengths; at the instance the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter apart only where they cannot meet at any instance of it: an object type apart from a type that neither it nor a supertype of it may be, and no `comprises` clause (`excludesAtMeet`, `OverloadedFunction.java:1041` at `84957e6ef`). The checker: `OverloadingOracle.excludes` asks `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.emptyED` beside `subtypeED` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:367`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:444`): the existential reduction's first premise alone, its bounds not read; and `meetEmptyWithBounds`, which reads each static parameter at the top of the meet as its declared bounds (`OverloadingOracle.scala:367`, `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:533`; F-277). On the interpreter's library `emptyED` is never reached: `subtypeED` shows all 691 meets the count stage tests empty. The two paths differ on two type parameters whose bounds exclude (row 786); on such a pair one of whose declarations has a `where` clause, which walk refuses and the checker accepts (row 787); and on a pair that walk's parameter check reads apart, reading an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type it is at some instance, as `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which walk loads and the checker refuses (row 788). Gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairExcludesTogetherWalk`, `GenericPairForcedObjectApartWalk`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/GenericPairExcludesTogether` and `GenericPairSharedSupertypeExclusion` (load, compile and dispatch), and `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairFreeArgumentWalk`, `GenericPairObjectSupertypeOverlapWalk` and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXGenericPairFreeArgument` (refused). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md` sections 2, 5 and 7.

- F-275 **Under walk, where the parameter-by-parameter check refuses two declarations with static parameters of their own and one lies inside the other, the load check reads the Return Type Rule at one instance of the outer one, and refuses the pair unless that instance stands for every instance that applies.** The instance is the one that walk's inference finds for the outer one at the inner one's parameter types. A check at that instance alone would load pairs that the rule refuses, since an argument of the inner one can select a smaller instance of the outer one. The instance stands for every applicable instance in two cases. In the first, each static parameter that the outer one's return type names is fixed by a static argument of one of its parameter types. In the second, the outer one returns one of its own type parameters, and the inner one meets one of two conditions. Either it returns a type parameter of its own that is the whole type of at least one of its parameters and appears in no other parameter type than those at positions where the outer one's parameter type is that returned type parameter; or, at such a position, it has an object type below which its return type lies. Otherwise walk refuses the pair, "fails the Return Type Rule" (F-257). With `trait Shape`, `trait Round extends Shape` and `object Circle extends Round`, it refuses `f[\T extends Shape\](x: T, y: T): T` beside `f[\U extends Round\](x: U, y: Round): Round`, and `f[\T extends Shape\](x: T): Box[\T\]` beside `f[\U extends Round\](x: U): Box[\U\]`; the compiled checker refuses both too. Gated by `tests/GenericReturnRuleOuterParamWalk` and `GenericReturnRuleInvariantWalk` (refused) and `GenericReturnRuleHoldsWalk` (load and dispatch). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-generic-pairs/SKEPTIC.md` section 2.

- F-366 **On both paths a numeral at a call leaves the declaration that fits it at its default only for one that its own coercion reaches and whose declared parameter types lie strictly below, by subtyping.** It builds P-46's rule for a numeral at a call. P-46 does not word the order: the worker that built the rule chose subtyping, and the curator has read that choice as landed and let it stand, without wording a decision of his own. So `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true`, and `u =/= 0` is `false`, for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, but on the compiled path until the switch-over the checker refuses `u =/= 0` at `RR32` and `RR64` (row 1059) and `u = 0` at `RR32`, an ambiguous coercion (row 528); `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`; `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`; a `case` clause `0` matches a zero `NN32`; and a program's own number type with a numeral coercion compares with a numeral by its own `=`. `Equality[\T\]` declares `opr =/=(self, other:T)` as the negation of the type's `=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:102`), which a type that extends `Equality` reaches before the `=/=` over `Any` (`:98`). The order between the declaration that the default fits and one that the coercion reaches is subtyping on the declared parameter types, not the coercion chapter's relation: `f(1.5)` beside `f(x: RR32)` and `f(x: RR64)` runs the `RR64` declaration, and `x^2` for an `RR64` keeps its integer power. A value's coercion is not ranked so. Where a call reaches two declarations only by coercion and they are not ordered, the one whose parameter the numeral's default fits as it is runs, whether they differ at the numeral alone or elsewhere too, so `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` checks against the one library at `RR64`'s juxtaposition. So a model line may compare a number of any type with a numeral, and write a float numeral beside an integer value, on both paths. The checker compares only where the declaration that fits has a numeral at a parameter that is not of the numeral's default type, so a call such as `i + 1` costs nothing more; the report says which choices walk keeps in its dispatch cache. Two departures: under walk a numeral beside a value typed `Any` is converted by the value's run-time type (row 1016), and on both paths a numeral at a bare type parameter's declaration does not go to a more specific one (row 1017). Source: `numeralAttempt` and `numeralTie` in `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:980-1021`, `:1066`, `:1143`; `bestMatchForNumerals` and `belowByNumerals` in `interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2422-2525`. Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralMostSpecificCompiled`, `compiler_tests/NumeralEqualsNumberCompiled`, `compiler_tests/NumeralTieDefaultCompiled`, `tests/NumeralMostSpecificWalk`, `tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk`, `tests/NotEqualNumeral`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-most-specific/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why" and "5. Points to report".

- F-373 **The compiled path runs `label` and `exit`: an exit is a thrown `LabelExit` that names one evaluation of its label block, and reaches it from a loop's body and from another task.** `CodeGen.forLabel` makes a new target for each evaluation of the block and takes, in a handler, the exits that name it; `CodeGen.forExit` throws `LabelExit.of(value, target)` (`runtimeSystem/LabelExit.java`). A function expression or a task whose body exits captures the target as it captures any immutable variable. A group of forked arms joins the arms that it forked before the exit passes it: at four threads every forked iteration of a parallel `for` runs to its end or to its own exit, and the label's value is the exit of the first arm in the arms' order; at one thread the iterations after the exit do not run. No `catch` clause takes an exit. An exit out of an `atomic` block commits the block's transaction (F-401). So the one library's `Indexed.indexOf` compiles in its own form (the test's `Holder.indexOf`), and row 81 is fixed. Three of the compiled answers were chosen as the path was built, and the curator has not decided them; walk answers each otherwise: which evaluation an exit leaves where the block is evaluated again inside itself, compiled the one in which the exit's function was made (row 1042); whether a `catch` of `Exception` takes an exit, compiled no (row 1040); and what an exit is after its label block has completed, compiled an uncaught `LabelExit` that ends the program (row 1041). Three limits stand, each with its test: a `finally` clause on the exit's way does not run (row 890); a label block as a call's later argument fails verification (row 322); a label block whose value joins a numeral with a number stops the code generator (row 340), though by P-50 the numeral takes the label's expected type; a program binds the numeral to a typed variable first. Test: `compiler_tests/LabelExitCompiled`, which fails with 'Can't compile Label' without `forLabel` and `forExit`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-label-exit/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Points to report reached".

- F-374 **A compiled object's `var` field lives in a cell that the object holds, and an atomic expression is its body in an atomic block.** On the compiled path a `var` value parameter or `var` field of an object is a `MutableFValue` cell in a `public final` JVM field, made by the constructor; each read and write checks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` and goes through the transaction or the cell, by the code of a top-level `var`, and a loop body or a function expression in the object's method captures the cell. The batch's planner chose the cell as a default, and the curator has not decided it. So an `atomic` block tracks a `var` field (row 319, fixed), and every access of one pays the transaction check, outside `atomic` too (row 641). A field without `var` holds its value and has no check. `atomic e` is compiled by `CodeGen.forAtomicBlock` on the block that holds `e` (row 875, fixed), with the block's limits (row 322); a numeral as its value at a place of declared type is refused or fails verification, since the checker carries no declared type into it (row 1043). So a change of the transaction's variable code reaches fields with no second edit, and a new kind of nested context must capture a var field's cell as it does a top-level `var`'s. A `value` object with a `var` field, which the specification forbids and nothing refuses (row 112), is not strictly equivalent to another built alike: `V(1) === V(1)` is `false`, since `SEQV` compares the cells by identity. The one library declares one, `Lazy` (`Library/Lazy.fss:18`). Tests: `compiler_tests/AtomicFieldCompiled`, `compiler_tests/VarFieldCapturedCompiled`, `compiler_tests/AtomicExprCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-atomic-expr-field/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The bytecode".

- F-401 **An exit out of an `atomic` block commits the block's transaction and keeps its writes, on both paths.** Compiled, the block's handler `BaseTask.leaveTransaction` commits on a `LabelExit` as `endTransaction` does at a normal end (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:303-309`); walk's `FortressTaskRunner.doItOnce` commits on a `LabelException` as at a normal end (`interpreter/evaluator/tasks/FortressTaskRunner.java:133-141`). A commit that fails runs the block again, as at a normal end, and an exception other than an exit still discards the writes. A nested block's commit hands its writes to the outer one, whose commit on the same exit stores them. Neither path tells an exit to an enclosing label from one to a label block that has completed, so such a late exit also commits the atomic blocks it passes (row 1041). Under walk an exit or an exception out of a `tryatomic` block that no `atomic` block encloses is wrapped in a `RuntimeException` and reaches neither its label nor a `catch` (rows 1110 and 1111). So a program may exit out of an atomic block (`Specification/basic/expressions/atomic.tex:59-63`). Tests: `tests/ExitOutOfAtomicWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/ExitOutOfAtomicCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-exit-out-of-atomic/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The tests: failing on the base, passing after".

- F-405 **Walk runs the generic dotted methods of one name that a trait or an object declares together, each as its instance at symbolic static arguments.** An object takes each generic method of a name, alone or beside others of the name, with one symbolic instantiation for each name and, per static parameter, kind and bounds, with the method's own static parameters in the bounds compared by position, not by name (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java`, `genericKey`): so an object's redeclaration of a trait's generic method at the same bounds under other names hides it, and two that differ in their bounds are overloads, except bounds that differ only in the api of a type of one simple name (row 1134). At load walk reads two such instances on their declared domains where one lies inside the other; a set of them whose overlap only a third covers is refused (row 1133), and so is, when an extending object's first instance is made, a nested pair of a generic trait's generic functional methods (row 780). An object that inherits two such methods of one name from two traits, neither more specific, with no declaration at their meet, loads and runs, where the Meet Rule refuses the set (row 1139). A call that writes no static argument infers them and dispatches among the instances, the inner declared domain first; a call that writes static arguments instantiates each generic method whose static parameters, by their number and kinds, take them, and chooses among those instances by the call's arguments, as a call of a top-level generic function does. A call on a receiver assumed at the trait stops (row 1126). Where a plain method shares the name with a generic one, a call that writes static arguments stops (row 744); of two generic functional methods of one name and one number of parameters, the second is never chosen (row 1123). Tests: `tests/GenericMethodOverloadArity.fss`, `GenericMethodOverloadSetWalk.fss`, `GenericOverloadStaticArgKindsWalk.fss`, `GenericMethodBoundsDifferWalk.fss`, whose object `Both` asserts walk's answers for row 1139's set, the departure. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check-generic-numeral/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Programs run old against new"; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-bounds-tuple-numeral-type/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".

content.content:
- F-97 **The gate's step 7 runs the interpreter's suite on the compiled path, each program judged by its own verdict, never against an earlier run (P-103).** It runs each program of `compile-ladder/gate/suite-compiled.tsv` under its library, and tries under both libraries each program of `ProjectFortress/tests/` that the batch added or changed; a listed program that fails is red unless a rung declared it leaving the list (`expectedMoves`), and a tried one that passes joins it. The list began with 197 programs, from the count on `4b0e3abd6a`. MicroGPT's eighteen components are no longer compiled there: at climb batch 35b's gate, their last measure, all 18 stopped at disambiguate under the prelude. Detail: `coordinator/tools/suite-compiled/README.md`.

- F-99 **The gate's thread count is pinned in the build file for the two suites, not in the calling shell.** `build.xml`'s `fastTrack` macro, which runs `testFast`, and its `systemShard` macro, which runs `testSystem`, set `FORTRESS_THREADS=4` (P-125). Without the pin, the suites would take the caller's count: half the CPUs if it is unset, or 1 under `env.sh` (F-203). `fastTrack` also pins `JAVA_FLAGS` to `-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, because a compiled test's run step takes its heap and stacks from it. With `JAVA_FLAGS` unset, a compiled test's run step (`bin/run`) gives its threads the JVM's default 1 MB stacks, and at four threads `library_tests/TimingRungT` overflowed in 8 of 12 runs (row 640). Detail: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 6.

- F-234 **A Fortress command that a worker types itself (`bin/fortress`, `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh`, or `java` of a Fortress main class) starts a fresh JVM, and that start costs too little to pay for a resident compiler.** A resident compiler is a background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did. The suites start one JVM for each test class, and one for each of `testSystem`'s four shards, not one for each test: the harness runs each test file inside its JVM. Only a compiled test's run step and a `.sh` test, such as `tests/concurrentPrinting.sh`, start another process. In one measurement over 267 worker transcripts, the one-off commands took 17.5 % of the wall time of the workers' shell commands, and the suites, builds and stages 47.8 %. Over the workers' whole running time, the one-off commands took 6.4 % (11.6 % if every wait that the measurement could not tie to a run was theirs). Removing their JVM start-up would save at most 1.8 % (P-150: no resident compiler is built). What runs inside the suites and the stages was not measured. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/fresh-jvm-commands.md`, "Summary", "What a resident compiler could save, at most" and "Decisions not taken".

- F-383 **Walk's harness counts a static error that a phase raises before the run, such as the disambiguator's, as a refusal at load, so a walk `.test` whose `load_` keys expect a refusal at load passes on such an error that its keys match.** `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java`, `InterpreterTest.thrownAtLoad`. Test: `tests/TypecaseUndefinedArmWalk.test`. A compiled refusal test is still `XXX`-named: a plain-named compile test is red whenever the compile reports errors. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-typecase-unbound-arm/REPORT.md`, "10. Decisions".

- F-404 **`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` copies `ProjectFortress/build` and, where the base build has it, `ProjectFortress/build-one`, so a seeded worktree's first `ant` target keeps the seeded caches.** The implementation's stamp covers `build-one` (`build.xml:400-402`, `:469-470`) and the script copies it, with `default_repository/caches-one` (`seed-worktree.sh:91-93`, `:101-108`); without it, in a worktree seeded from a base build that has `build-one` the first target prints 'Sources and build as the last build left them? no', rebuilds the Scala and starts both `default_repository/caches` and `caches-one` again, empty; a compiled run under `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` before it stops, 'java.lang.Error: The type ZZ of the library that the compiled path reads is not compiled over com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ of the run-time classes on the class path'. No test: in a worktree seeded from a base build that has `build-one`, the first `ant compileAll` prints 'Sources and build as the last build left them? yes' and keeps both caches (`88f286dc30`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-boolean-equivalence/REPORT.md`, "Defects, and their homes".

- F-240 **The checker's count stage takes about 65 s and its distance stage 117 s at the last landed gate, climb batch 36's.** At climb batch 15b's gate they took 325 s and 1,075 s; the solver's memos (F-235) make most of the difference, not load. Its rise from about 90 s at climb batch 21b's gate is the `FortressLibrary` component's check now run to its end, past its cleared type errors into the export check, not load: rung runs that stopped at those errors took 91 s and 99 s, runs past them 149 s and 151 s, one run each. Since climb batch 21b the checker checks every symbolic operator (F-281), which costs the count stage about 15 to 25 % by its rung's timings of its base and its head in one session. From climb batch 22's gate to climb batch 26's it stayed between about 150 s and 180 s. The count table records no seconds, so its time is the file times of the gate's log; the distance stage (`FortressLibrary` 75 s), over fourteen components, ran at a start load of 0.29, then beside the first minutes of `testFast`, so its time is one under that suite's load, against 130 s (85 s) at 0.55 at climb batch 35b's. Both stages about halved at climb batch 27's gate, and no run measured why: each gate ran each stage once, and neither the emptied `Number` (F-324) nor the distance's check stopped at `Char` (F-54) is shown to be the cause. Load can lengthen a stage more than twofold: climb batch 16's merged code took 217 s for the distance stage at its gate, at a load average of 3.3, and nearly the same code took 574 s at 4.6 to 5.3. So a time compares only with one taken under a like load. Source: the file times of the gate's log and `compile-ladder/climb-batch-36/gate/distance.txt`. Detail: `reviews/batch-31-review.md`, section 4; `reviews/batch-32-review.md`, section 4; `reviews/batch-27-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-26-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-25-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-24-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-23-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-22c-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-22-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-21b-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-17-review.md`, section 1; `reviews/batch-16-review.md`, section 2.

- F-221 **The compiled checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each enclosing declaration's parameter type, where the enclosing call is not accepted otherwise.** It builds P-51 under P-49, so a declaration that accepts the call as written is never passed over. A reduction's plain-bounded big operator, an argument of `__bigOperator` once desugared, so takes the reduction's expected type; one whose bound names its parameter takes that type, else its body's (F-364). A chain `a OPLUS b OPLUS c` that only the retry makes acceptable to a multifix declaration now runs it, not the binary one. Walk gives such an argument no expected type (row 705). Gated by `compiler_tests/InferCallArgument*` and `InferBigOperatorExpectedType`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-argument-context/REPORT.md` sections 1, 5 and 8, and `SKEPTIC.md` finding 5.

- F-56 **The compiled checker keeps the expected type, for inferring the call's static arguments, at a call written `f(x)`, which the parser builds as a tight juxtaposition: `f` and `(x)` with no space between.** It keeps it at a method call and an operator too; F-87 lists the other contexts. Only desugarings reach the `fnApp = true` path of `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Operators.scala:88-90`, so an edit of that path alone changes nothing for a call written `f(x)`. Gated by `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes`. Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/measure-D.md` section 1.

- F-55 **Static arguments are inferred with coercion on both paths: the compiled checker from the arguments' static types and the expected type, walk from their run-time types.** So a mixed-width call takes the narrowest type into which its arguments convert, as P-74 decides. F-73 gives the checker's rule and F-137 walk's; F-87 lists where the checker has an expected type. Under walk, a typed binding converts a call's result after the call and does not fix the call's static arguments: `a: BoxK[\ZZ64\] = wrapK(3)` infers `T` from `3` as `ZZ32` and is refused, since no coercion converts a `BoxK[\ZZ32\]` (row 510). A parameter with no written bound is bounded by `Any` on both paths, so a parameter that nothing fixes takes `Any` (F-78). Gated by `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes` and `tests/InferCoercionRungK`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-inference-checker/REPORT.md` section 3.2; `compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 9.

- F-108 **The interpreter's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that is not a property of the program.** Without the flags below, as `bin/fortress` and the suites run walk, the order varies from run to run. With three JVM flags set, `-XX:+UseSerialGC -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1`, the order is fixed for a given library, and a library edit can flip it. The three were always set together, so which of them fixes the order is not known. The harness reads only that the `XXX` test fails, not the order. Row 430 records this order, and no gate stage compares the message (P-103). Evidence: observed: `compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/JUDGE.md` sections 3 to 5.

- F-105 **`testSystem`'s four shards are one suite split by sorted index, so per-shard counts are not comparable across a change to the interpreter corpus and only their sum is.** Shard i takes every file whose index in the sorted list is i modulo 4, so an added file moves every later one. `gate_compare` in `coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` sums the `system-<i>` rows before it compares. Detail: `compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md` section 1.

- F-151 **In the interpreter's library, `Vector`, `Matrix` and their factories and operators bound their element type by `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.** `Number` declares no arithmetic, so the compiled checker accepts the bodies' arithmetic only through `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`. `Number` stays in the bound, though it has no `comprises` clause now (F-324). The four juxtapositions of a vector or a matrix with a scalar `T`, in either order, stand beside the library's juxtapositions with a `String`, and the checker finds no error in them (F-53); no run measures what now keeps a scalar `T` apart from `String`. The vector norm is declared at each of the eight number types, by its own `asFloat` (F-324). The eight number types meet the bound. `Number` itself and the numeral types do not, since none is a ring at its own type. So `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not a well-formed type, and `array1` and `array2` have no branch for `Number`: called at `Number`, they give a plain array at run time, not a vector or a matrix (F-229). The checker accepts a call whose argument's type is built from the caller's own type parameter under the same bound, such as the norm's `squaredNorm(me)` (F-227). The scalar extension, the eight operators between an array and a scalar, has bounds of its own, also with `Number` (F-119). Gated under walk by `tests/ArrayElementAlgebra.fss`. The bound is the default that `reviews/array-fork2-judgement.md` recommended. Detail: that judgement, sections 2.5 (what `Number`'s `comprises` clause gives), 2.9, way 3 (the ring alone, measured) and 4 (the bound and its cost).

- F-159 **In probes of 2026-09-29, a generic factory with a written static argument selected a store written for `RR64` alone, through a witness `typecase` whose branch result was passed through `cast`, on both paths.** A store is the object that holds an array's elements. A witness is `__thrower[\X\]`, a function of type `() -> X` that is never called; a `typecase` on it chooses a branch by the type `X`. The probes declared their own one-method trait `Arr[\T\]` and two stores, `DStore` for `RR64` and a generic `BStore`; they used none of the library's array traits, and the compiled runs used the compiler's own prelude. A witness `typecase` whose `RR64` branch returns `DStore` ran under walk. The compiled checker refused the body, whose type is the union `OR(DStore,BStore[\T\])`, against the declared result `Arr[\T\]`. With that branch's result passed through `cast[\Arr[\T\]\]`, as the library's `additiveIdentity` does, it checked. Both paths then gave `DStore` for `mk[\RR64\](r)`, with `r: RR64`, and `BStore` for `mk[\ZZ32\](z)`. A plain factory for `RR64` beside the generic one, called from generic code, was accepted by the compiled checker and dispatched to the plain declaration. Walk refused that pair at load; its present load check (F-27), which reads a generic declaration beside a plain one on their declared domains, has not been run on it. The library's `array1` and `array2` take a witness of their result type, not of the element type, for the reason F-229 gives. It bears on array decision A, how an array of a number type gets its unboxed store, which is open (P-85). No gated test holds it, and the probes are in the history before `84aef6a4f`. Detail: `reviews/array-design-ways.md` sections 0 and 3.

- F-229 **`array1` and `array2` give a vector and a matrix only at the eight number types, chosen by a `typecase` over a witness of their result type; at any other element type they give a plain array.** The branches are `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`; each builds the array at that type and returns it through `cast`, in `additiveIdentity`'s shape. `Array1` and `Array2` are invariant, so a branch matches only its own number type exactly. `Number` and `AnyIntegral` get a plain array, since `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not well-formed under the element bound `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` of `Vector` and `Matrix` (F-151). The specification's "Array Expressions" makes an array of `Number` elements a vector (row 729, contested). Under walk, a type parameter inferred from a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `RR64` value is that type, so it gets a vector (`tests/ArrayInferredElementVectorWalk`). The witness is of the result type because a witness of the element type failed while walk's `ZZ32` values were of a native object `Int`, now gone (F-379): at `T = Int`, `() -> Int` matched the `ZZ32` branch, and the `cast` of the `ZZ32` vector to an array of `Int` threw `CastError` (row 722, the same cast in `openRange`). Gated under walk by `tests/ArrayFactoryNumberTypes` and `ArrayFactoryAbstractNumber`. The distance stage measures the compiled checker's acceptance; it reports, and does not turn the gate red. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-factories/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the change), 3 and 4 (the ways measured).

- F-264 **In the interpreter's library, nine `Vector` and `Matrix` operators and three branches of the array factories get their declared type through the function `cast`, and so does the sub-array that `Array2`'s column and row subscripts pass to `Col` and `Row`.** `cast[\T\](x)` returns `x` if it has type `T`, and raises `CastError` if not (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:33-37`). The operators are `Vector`'s `+`, binary and unary `-`, `scale` and `pmul`, and `Matrix`'s `+`, binary and unary `-` and `scale`. Each builds its result with the inherited `map` or `ivmap`, typed `Array1` or `Array2`, and so through `replica`, the method that makes an array of the same layout. The factory branches are those of `__builtinFactory1`, `__immutableFactory1` and `__builtinFactory2` for an array whose lowest indices are 0, each cast to its factory's declared result type. The subscripts are `a[:, j]` and `a[i, :]`. Each builds its sub-array with a range subscript, which answers an unsized `Array`, and the cast gives it the sized `Array2` that the field of `Col` or `Row` takes. Five bodies build with `fill` or `tabulate` and need no cast, since `Vector` and `Matrix` redeclare those two at their own type (F-158): the factories `vector(v)`, `tabulatedVector` and `matrix(v)`, and `Matrix`'s `rmul` and `lmul`. So the compiled checker accepts all these bodies (the distance stage). Under walk each cast holds at the eight number types (`tests/VectorMatrixCastsWalk.fss`). A `Vector` whose `replica` answers an array that is not a `Vector`, or a `Matrix` whose `replica` answers one that is not a `Matrix`, raises `CastError` at the nine operators. When the casts landed, no walk value moved in the 42 test files that use the array family, compared value by value, or in four array demos; every test of the interpreter's suite passed, and so did microGPT's quick pair. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-array-sites/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 5 (each change with its sites; walk's runs); `compile-ladder/rung-array-sites/SKEPTIC.md` sections 2 (the four demos) and 3, finding 3 (the `CastError` case).

- F-279 **Under walk an `Array2` or `Array3` based above zero slices like a 0-based one, except a shifted `Array2`.** `Array2.subarray` and `Array3.subarray` hand their 0-based views the offset less the base, and `Array3`'s `[:]` passes its base, as `Array1`'s do (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2999`, `:3401`, `:3380`; `:2711`). `SubArray2`'s own `subarray` subtracts the output base instead of its own (`:3083`, row 808), so a slice of a shifted `Array2` still reads the wrong elements, and a shift of a slice, a column, a row or a shifted `Array2` ends in Java's `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Tests: `Array2SliceAtNonzeroBase`, `Array3SliceAtNonzeroBase`, `XXXArray2ShiftedSlice`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-slices-list-equality/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 5.

- F-368 **Under walk a top-level array literal with a declared type is built into the library array of that type, in the variable's cell.** `LazilyEvaluatedCell.getValueNull` builds an immutable variable's literal when the cell is first forced, so a reader above the declaration, an importer and `forVarDecl4`'s type check all see the array; `BuildEnvironments.forVarDecl4` builds a `var` variable's. Both call `LHSEvaluator.topLevelArray`, which runs the block's code, `libraryArray`. So under walk a table of the model can be a top-level literal with a declared type, as `shp: ZZ32[9] = [...]`; the code generator compiles no array literal (the `fortress-repo` skill's `references/compiler.md`), so such a line does not compile. The declared size is checked only at the top level, by `forVarDecl4`; a block binds a literal of another size (row 1022). A field declaration of an object takes the same code. An untyped top-level literal stays a paste (row 49); a `var` bound in a block to a literal is immutable (row 1024), and a literal assigned to a variable is not built (row 1025). Tests: `tests/ObjectFieldArrayLiteral.fss`, `tests/TopLevelArrayLiteral.fss`, `TopLevelArrayLiteralSize.fss`, `TopLevelArrayLiteralElement.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-toplevel-array-literal/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-379 **The one library and walk declare `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` each as one value object, and a program's object below one is refused at load.** P-178's one-library half holds: the objects are `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:384`, `:846`, `:951`, `:1063`, `:1170`, and walk builds their native values from the glue classes of the same names, such as `interpreter/glue/prim/ZZ32.java`, found by a table (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java:459-470`). No `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` or `UnsignedLong` is declared in the library or used by walk's Java; a typecase arm at one of those names is refused on both paths, 'Int is undefined.' (row 959, fixed; F-382). So `asif` at one of the five is the identity, and `object Mine extends ZZ32` is refused, 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'. Walk's load check reads pairs over the five as over objects: a valid generic-beside-plain pair at `ZZ64` loads (row 550, fixed), and so do two kinds of invalid pair: a plain declaration with no written return type beside a generic one (row 1044), and two plain lists whose more specific one returns a type not below the other's, against the Subtype Rule, such as `f(x: Number): ZZ32` beside `f(x: ZZ64): String` (row 697). With `NN32` and `RR32`, objects already, seven of the eight number types are objects, `QQ` the trait; the compiler's prelude declares the same seven as value objects (F-388). Tests: `tests/NumberTypesAreObjectsWalk.fss`, `tests/NumberTypeExtendRefusedWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-objects/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "What a program sees differently".

- F-157 **An array is a trait with `get` and `put`, and a view is an object that implements it over other storage; this is the language's own idiom for a view of a runtime shape, as the library's own `TransposedMatrix` is.** Under walk, a subtype of `Matrix` that overrides `mul` gets its own product through the library's `Matrix` juxtaposition and `DOT`, which forward to `mul`. It needs no api line, since walk dispatches the method on the receiver's run-time type; the override was measured under walk only. In two measurements under walk at `b176a4b79`, views through the library cost more. On lifting a function over the rows of a 64 × 16 matrix, the row slice `m[i,:]` took five times as long as a six-line user view (row 298). The library's product with a diagonal that is a plain `Matrix` view, without the override, took 13 times as long as a row-scaling operator at n = 16, and 58 to 63 times at n = 64 (row 299, which says 54). Detail: `reviews/c4-flatarrays-review.md` section 1 (the idiom); `run-c4/probes/vocabulary/diag-override.md`, "Result" (the override) and "Timings against row 299" (the ratios).

- F-166 **On the topics of its Types chapter, such as the exclusion rule and covariance, the team's latest word is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`.** The restart, `Documentation/Specification/`, was never adopted. Its Types chapter restates the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" and adds `covariant`. On the rest of static parameters, and on traits beyond a stub, exceptions, components and the numeric library, `Specification/` is the only statement. Which text governs is the curator's: `Specification/` stays the standard, the Types chapter is cited beside it, and `covariant` is future work (P-25). The type group's POPL 2019 paper is later than both (F-271). Detail: `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` section 6 and its "Coordinator's check (2026-09-26)".

- F-167 **The specification states instantiation exclusion and keeps each example that the rule refuses, marked "Not allowed"; the calculi of Appendix A carry a callout that they predate the rule.** It builds P-97. It also bars a `where`-clause variable from an `extends` clause's static arguments. The covariance example, the empty list, the empty optional value and the root type `Object`'s algebraic supertraits each stand beside the library's shape, which runs on both paths except `Nothing[\String\]` on the compiled prelude (row 331). A subtrait of every instantiation stays as the counterexample that introduces the rule, and the internal appendix's refused examples get a callout each. The checker does not yet refuse two cases: an object that extends two instantiations that differ only in a `bool` argument (row 406), and one that extends two instantiations of one trait where one instantiation's argument is the object's own static parameter, such as `O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` (row 414). Detail and examples: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; its section 4.2 (the calculi's callout).

- F-271 **The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives P-48's instance rule, and its soundness proof does not cover the library's F-bounded functions, such as `SUM` and `BIG MAX`.** By P-48's rule, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes the intersection of its upper bounds. The paper is later than both the specification and the team's restart (F-166). Its calculus does not let a method type parameter occur in an upper bound, so F-bounded method parameters are outside it. It also leaves out top-level functions and functional methods, among other limits. `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` checks the curator's decisions against the paper. Detail: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md` sections 6 and 8.

- F-273 **The specification gives the run-time instance of a generic declaration that dispatch reaches, and that the static call did not select, by the POPL 2019 paper's rule.** It builds P-48. A declaration that the static call selected runs at the instance inferred for the call (F-173). Where an argument's value fixes a type parameter, as a value of `Tag[\X\]` fixes `X`, the rule and both paths agree. Where a type parameter is a parameter's whole type, the argument's run-time type only bounds it from below. The rule then gives it its declared bound, narrowed by what the call's static type requires of the return type. The dispatch paragraph's callout says that both paths take the argument's run-time type there instead. Walk always will, since it has no static types (P-48). The compiled path does so because its dispatcher is not given the call's static type (row 538, the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed`). The callout also says that the compiled path does not yet run the paragraph's second example, a generic declaration beside a plain one, reached through an argument of static type `Any` (row 496). Detail: `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:312-349`, in the chapter "Overloading and Multiple Dispatch"; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 5 and 6.

- F-174 **The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters, and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration over all its instances within its bounds.** It states P-45 and P-42. The section "Declarations with Static Parameters" states the OOPSLA 2011 paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet. It gives one more restriction as the compiled path's, not the language's. Where one generic declaration is more specific than another with as many static parameters, the two must declare them of the same kinds, position by position. Also, the more specific one's return type must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are matched by position, so the checker refuses an override whose return type reorders its static parameters (row 398, fixed). The section "Principles of Overloading" forbids overloading a functional whose single parameter's type is a type parameter with the bound `Any` written, as `T extends Any`. A type parameter with no `extends` clause, whose bound is also `Any`, is exempt. Both paths refuse such an overload: the checker in `OverloadingChecker.checkBoundAny`, and walk since row 534's fix. Neither path runs every set that the rules allow. Appendix I's entry "Overloading with static parameters" names the sets that each path fails. In row 1048, the checker refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over a tuple of object types, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)`. In row 537, the code generator fails on two generic declarations whose bounds differ. In row 539, walk refuses at load the 2019 paper's valid set over an array list and a list. In rows 779 and 780, walk fails on two generic functional methods one of whose declared domains lies inside the other's: in a trait or object without static parameters it refuses them at load, and in a trait with static parameters it stops with an error when an extending object's first instance is made. Detail: `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:134-150` and `:531-674`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.

- F-179 **Tasks and transactions are implemented twice, in `interpreter/evaluator/` and in `runtimeSystem/`, independently.** A fix in one copy does not reach the other: row 302's fix is in the compiled copy only. Detail: `coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md`, "B.11 The runtime".

- F-181 **The code generator compiles a function, method, object or trait declaration that carries a `where` clause in its own header, emitting nothing for the clause, and refuses every function or method with a contract (row 701).** The clause's constraints are the checker's. A trait's or object's contract does not reach the refusal: the disambiguator drops it (row 781); F-255 says how each path reads a `where` clause on an `extends` entry (row 774). Walk checks a function's `requires` clause and raises `CallerViolation`. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet", gives the refusal and the constructs that the code generator has no case for; an array comprehension has no case either. A local function compiles as a closure, except in the forms that F-320 names. A trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size, of `NatParam`'s shape, compiles; a call that opens its value to the size fails verification (row 307). Where a generic type that such a clause lists gives a member's body, the member compiles too (row 812, fixed; F-384). A function's or method's own clause that introduces a `where`-clause variable compiles, and the compiled call dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (row 867). Tests: `compiler_tests/WhereBoundFunctionCompiled`, `WhereBoundMethodCompiled`, `WhereBoundObjectCompiled`, `WhereBoundTraitMethodCompiled`, `ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodCompiled`; `XXXFunctionContractCodeGeneration`; the `XXXNatOpenRun` pair; the `XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled` pair. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-codegen-where/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 2 and 5.

- F-183 **The compiled path's only array-like types are `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`, two hand-written Java classes declared only in its prelude and absent from the specification.** Each element access is boxed. No gated test makes or indexes a `ZZ32Vector` at run time. Gated tests make a `StringVector`, store two strings in it with `putValue` and assert its rendering (`compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS`), and read `args`, which is one (`Compiled2`). Passed to a generic object's constructor, either type fails at load: its descriptor class is `RTTIv`, where stamped code asks for `RTTIc`. Row 408 and `compiler_tests/XXXVecCtorLoad` hold this for a `ZZ32Vector`; the probe measured a `StringVector` too. A native helper cannot take a Java array, since the wrapper generator skips such methods. Detail: `compiler-probes/vectors/vectors.md` sections 1, 3 (step 9), 6 and 7.

- F-184 **A generic object referenced without its static arguments is a static error on the compiled path, and the checker never consults the expected type for it.** `b: Box[\ZZ32\] = Box` fails as an ill-formed type, and a bare `Empty` as an argument or a field's default as an internal error, `T is not in the kind env`. Walk fails on both. Writing the static argument avoids both. So a bare `Nothing` compiles only against the compiled prelude's own `Nothing` (row 331, P-90). Detail: `compiler-probes/maybe-inference/inference.md`.

- F-355 **The pure-Java microGPT that P-7 names as the baseline is in `java-baseline/`: one training step at batch 1 takes about 0.10 ms after warm-up without the Adam update, and 0.113 ms with it.** It is the flat program line for line, in `double[]` and plain loops on one thread with the JDK alone, and it passes the flat program's 7 quick and 40 full checks against the same reference files at the same tolerances. Measured once, on a shared machine of 4 CPUs with OpenJDK 25: fork medians of 100.8 to 104.0 µs for one step in 10 fresh JVMs; as cold processes, 72 ms for the five-step run and 77 ms for the quick check. It is the careful scalar Java, not the fastest: HotSpot vectorises none of its matrix products, and the Vector API in the products alone gives 75 µs. In one session on that machine a step with Adam took 0.113 ms in this program, 0.20 ms in NumPy, 13 ms under dzaima/APL and 132 ms in pure Python, which computes 7.3 positions a step against 16. So a compiled Fortress step is measured against about 0.1 ms, and pure Python is about 1,200 times slower than this baseline. The program keeps the arithmetic of the Fortress source; only a sum of more than 16 terms is added in another order than the library's. No test checks the timings. Commands: `java-baseline/run.sh` and `run.sh bench`. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "4. Timings of the baseline" and "5. Vectorisation: what HotSpot did with the baseline's loops"; `java-baseline/python-comparison.md`, "1. The answer".

- F-356 **In the fork/join shape that the library and the compiled runtime give parallel work, a Java model of microGPT's step with unboxed arrays runs 19 to 80 times slower than plain loops at the library's grains, and 1.4 to 4.8 times slower with the matrix product stopped at blocks of 16.** The library's range stops its split at 16 elements (`grainSize`, `Library/RangeInternals.fss`; P-175), and its matrix product splits down to single elements (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3129-3187`). The model is the baseline of F-355 with its vocabulary on a `ForkJoinPool` and plain loops at the leaves, so its times are a floor for compiled Fortress with this structure. At the library's grains a step takes 19 to 32 times the plain step on one thread, 55 times on two and 80 on four. Threads gain only from a product of about 128 by 128 with blocks of 64, and a dot product only from about 260,000 elements with a grain of 1,024; the model's products are 16 by 16 to 64 by 16. So at microGPT's sizes the library's parallel shape costs time at any thread count, and the matrix product's missing grain is the largest part of the cost. Measured once on a shared machine of 4 CPUs; every configuration passes the checks. Commands: `java-baseline/run.sh steps`, `kernels` and `scale`. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime".

- F-357 **`FlatData.parseFloat`, the flat program's reader of its weight files, is not correctly rounded: 699 of the 4,192 initial parameters differ from the double nearest to their decimal text, by up to 2 ulp.** It accumulates the mantissa digit by digit in a double and scales once. So a port of the model must port the parser to start from the same parameters, as the Java baseline does (F-355). No check depends on it: the loader check reads its reference through the same parser. Shown on the Java port of the parser, which keeps its arithmetic, by `java-baseline/run.sh parse`: '4192 numbers, 699 differ from Double.parseDouble, the worst by 2.0 ulp'; no Fortress was run for it. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "3. What could not be matched, and what was chosen".

- F-350 **On the compiled path the arms of a parallel `do`, the elements of a tuple, the operands of an operator and the arguments of a call fork through one method, `CodeGen.genParallelExprs`, which joins every arm that it forked before an exception leaves the group; arguments fork where `ParallelismAnalyzer` marked the argument tuple.** The exception that leaves is that of the first arm, in the arms' order, that threw; when an exception leaves, an arm not yet forked is not run, and a `VirtualMachineError` leaves without the joins (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:113-131`, `joinIfForked`). The analyzer marks no call written in the prelude's files, so the prelude's reductions run in sequence until the switch-over (row 982); the one library's parallel `ZZ32` range splits only a range of more than `grainSize`, 16, elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:20`, `:1320`, `:1337`). What it means: compiled against the one library, a reduction over more than 16 elements will fork its halves, and an exception leaves no arm running. By reading, not run: microGPT's vectors are 16, 16, 4 and 4 wide (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:17`), so a reduction over one of them forks nothing on either path. Tests: `compiler_tests/AlsoArmThrowsJoinsCompiled`, `CallArgumentsForkCompiled`, `tests/ParRangeGrainWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-forked-arguments/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Points to report reached"; the model's widths against the grain: `reviews/batch-30-review.md`, "2. The three forks that landed at a default".
